abstract:
Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.

Project page: https://geometric-abstraction.github.io

sections.body: Frontier multimodal models can reason about 3D scenes and drive manipulation directly, but closed-loop use often requires re-reading raw images as the scene changes. The paper asks whether an agent must reinterpret the visual scene at every decision step. Its interface models scene geometry as typed 3D object parts, such as centers, vertices, edges and oriented surfaces, each with a timestamp and an evidence status: observed, inferred, or unavailable. Symbolic references and geometric operators let policies compose actions, while compact textual checkpoints report updated coordinates and metric goal residuals after each action. The authors study the interface in offline policy synthesis and in continuous online execution, reporting faster policy acquisition, higher multi-step construction completion, and fewer repeated multimodal queries.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Closed-loop manipulation need not reinterpret raw images at every step; the paper proposes a typed 3D geometric abstraction instead.

sections.body: Related work falls into groups. VoxPoser, ReKep, KALM, RT-Affordance and ATK use 3D value maps, relational keypoint constraints, or extracted affordances as intermediate representations. Code as Policies and Inner Monologue compose perception and control APIs in code and add closed-loop language feedback. Later agentic frameworks extend program synthesis through coding-agent benchmarks, modular policy graphs, skill libraries, and execution-driven repair. The authors state that these works focus on how policies are synthesized, orchestrated or repaired. Their contribution is the spatial state interface: symbolic references are re-grounded after each action, and metric goal residuals and evidence status are returned as text, so later decisions reason over the observed post-action scene.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior keypoint, value-map and code-policy methods focus on synthesis or repair, not on a persistent evidence-aware scene state for each action.

sections.body: The interface grounds typed references from calibrated RGB-D observations at execution time. Shape information acquired at initialization persists, but object pose must be re-estimated from a current observation rather than copied from the previous state or inferred from commanded motion. Elements the observation cannot support are marked unavailable. The operators are reference, relation, align and checkpoint. The align operator returns the minimum-angle rotation and reports the remaining twist. Support predicates return unknown when a required surface is unobserved, and a true result is treated as a geometric candidate, not as evidence of contact or stability. For a target position $g_{i}$, the checkpoint reports the residual $e_{t}=g_{i}-p_{i}(t)$; when the object is occluded, the residual is marked unavailable instead of being computed from a stale pose.
sections.heading: Geometric Abstraction as a Reasoning-to-Action Interface
sections.headline: Typed references are grounded from RGB-D at execution time and returned as checkpoints with metric residuals and evidence status.

sections.body: All experiments run in simulation with an SO-100 robot arm carrying calibrated side and wrist RGB-D cameras. Both conditions receive the same task specification, sensor access, actuator interface and initial skills, and no simulator object poses or private evaluator state. The Pixel Reasoning condition reasons directly from visual observations, while the Geometric Abstraction condition also receives grounded geometric references and textual checkpoints. The first regime tests policy synthesis over repeated rollouts on three manipulation tasks, with held-out evaluation on 100 layouts per task. The second tests continuous online execution in a single non-resetting episode on three tasks, with 50 paired layouts each and a 200 s wall-clock budget that includes model waiting time.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Geometric abstraction improves policy acquisition and online completion in simulation while reducing images sent to the model.

sections.body: The evaluation is limited to simulated table-top manipulation with regular object geometries. The authors name real-world deployment as the essential next step, to test performance under realistic sensor noise, heavy occlusion and camera calibration drift. They used lightweight CPU-based geometric estimators on purpose, leaving learned 3D perception and articulated or deformable objects for future work. They argue the main benefit is supplying direct, actionable spatial state across the reasoning-action loop, rather than shortening prompts. Vision-language model assistance could broaden shape initialization for new object categories, but its one-time cost must be counted against execution and amortized. Decoupling local grounding from reasoning could also let fast text-only language models act on verified state.
sections.heading: Limitations and Discussion
sections.headline: Results cover simulated tabletop scenes with regular shapes; real-world sensing, occlusion, and new object categories remain untested.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the question of whether agentic robot policies must reinterpret visual observations at every decision step. The authors report that, across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, an explicit geometric abstraction improves manipulation completion and substantially reduces repeated multimodal queries. Symbolic references are paired with metric values refreshed from local RGB-D observations, so visual sensing stays active in the control loop without requiring the language model to process images at every step. Direct visual reasoning is kept for on-demand use.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Explicit geometric state is presented as a practical substrate for agentic robot policies, with images used on demand.

sections.body: Appendix A gives Table 2, with held-out test success and cumulative tokens per revision for each task and condition across five training chains. Appendix B gives Table 3, with completed episodes, capped completion time, model time, tokens, requests and attached images for the 50 paired online layouts per task, plus notes on audited repeats. The evaluation notes state the success criteria, including a five-second stable hold on the construction tasks and a two-second hold on Ring-on-peg. Appendix C describes the implementation: pixels are back-projected into world coordinates, fixed estimators run on the CPU, and each symbolic reference stores coordinates, physical units, timestamps and an evidence status.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists single-policy test tables, online outcome and cost tables, evaluation criteria, and the geometric implementation details.
